newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan welcomes U.S. backing for landmine initiative.
newsitem.headline: Annan welcomes U.S. backing for landmine initiative.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan welcomed Tuesday an announcement that the United States would take part in the so-called "Ottawa process" negotiations on a treaty banning anti-personnel landmines.
"He is convinced that such a treaty is urgently needed to put an end to the enormous suffering caused every day by this indiscriminate weapon," a statement issued through a U.N. spokesman said.

"The action by the United States comes at a critical moment, as arrangements are being made to open formal negotiations in Oslo on September 1. The secretary-general hopes that the Oslo conference will succeed in concluding a truly comprehensive ban, which will come to the (U.N.) General Assembly for endorsement at its coming session. He looks forward to opening the treaty for signature in Ottawa in December," the statement said.
Annan also hoped for progress in parallel efforts being made at the U.N. Conference on Disarmament in Geneva to achieve "universality of a total ban on these horrific weapons."
A White House statement Monday said the United States "will participate in the Ottawa process negotiations on a treaty banning anti-personnel land mines."

Washington rejected the Canadian initiative early this year, saying it left little room for exceptions sought by U.S. military commanders. Instead, it favored the U.N. Conference on Disarmament as the focus of U.S. policy.
U.S. officials have since concluded that not enough progress was being made in Geneva.

But tough negotiations are still likely as Washington insists on an exception for the Korean peninsula, where it has 37,000 troops in South Korea facing the threat of a possible invasion from communist North Korea.
It also wants to delay a ban on "smart" land mines, which self-destruct after a set time period, until it has developed alternative weapons.
U.S. officials estimate 9,600 people are killed by land mines worldwide every year and 14,000 are wounded, double the number of injuries logged in 1980.
The Canadian initiative promises a treaty banning the use, export, production and stockpiling of anti-personnel land mines but does not cover anti-vehicle or anti-tank mines.
